current_example.title: Example: Identifying Equivalence Classes Containing a Given Element

q-221714.name: Question 1
q-221714.problem:
Consider the equivalence relation $∼$ on $R,$ defined by $x∼y$ if ${x}^{4}={y}^{4}.$ Which of the following are in the equivalence class $[-1]?$

I. $1$

II. $4$

III. $-1$
q-221714.worked_solution:
The equivalence class $[-1]$ consists of the elements that are equivalent to $-1$ under the given equivalence relation. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}[-1] & =\{x\in R\,|\,x∼-1\} \\  & =\{x\in R\,|\,{x}^{4}=(-1)^{4}\} \\  & =\{x\in R\,|\,{x}^{4}-1=0\} \\  & =\{x\in R\,|\,({x}^{2}+1)({x}^{2}-1)=0\} \\  & =\{x\in R\,|\,{x}^{2}-1=0\} \\  & =\{x\in R\,|\,{x}^{2}=1\} \\  & =\{-1,1\}.\end{aligned}
$$

We see that $-1$ and $1$ are in $[-1],$ while $4$ is not.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

q-77200.name: Question 2
q-77200.problem:
Consider the equivalence relation $∼$ on $R,$ defined by $x∼y$ if ${x}^{3}={y}^{3}.$ Which of the following are in the equivalence class $[8]?$

I. $-2$

II. $2$

III. $8$
q-77200.worked_solution:
The equivalence class $[8]$ consists of the elements that are equivalent to $8$ under the given equivalence relation. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}[8] & =\{x\in R\,|\,x∼8\} \\  & =\{x\in R\,|\,{x}^{3}={8}^{3}\} \\  & =\{x\in R\,|\,x=8\} \\  & =\{8\}.\end{aligned}
$$

We see that $8$ is in $[8],$ while $-2$ and $2$ are not.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only".

q-76892.name: Question 3
q-76892.problem:
Consider the equivalence relation $∼$ on $R,$ defined by $x∼y$ if $\operatorname{sin}⁡x=\operatorname{sin}⁡y.$ Which of the following are in the equivalence class $[-\pi ]?$

I. $0$

II. $-\frac{\pi }{2}$

III. $\pi $
q-76892.worked_solution:
The equivalence class $[-\pi ]$ consists of the elements that are equivalent to $-\pi $ under the given equivalence relation. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}[-\pi ] & =\{x\in R\,|\,x∼-\pi \} \\  & =\{x\in R\,|\,\operatorname{sin}⁡x=\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\pi )\} \\  & =\{x\in R\,|\,\operatorname{sin}⁡x=0\} \\  & =\{…,-2\pi ,-\pi ,0,\pi ,2\pi ,…\}.\end{aligned}
$$

We see that $0$ and $\pi $ are in $[-\pi ],$ while $-\frac{\pi }{2}$ is not.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

q-221718.name: Question 4
q-221718.problem:
Consider the equivalence relation $∼$ on $Z,$ defined by $x∼y$ if $7\,|\,(x-y).$ Which of the following are in the equivalence class $[5]?$

I. $12$

II. $-4$

III. $-2$
q-221718.worked_solution:
The equivalence class $[5]$ consists of the elements that are equivalent to $5$ under the given equivalence relation. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}[5] & =\{x\in Z\,:\,x∼5\} \\  & =\{x\in Z\,:\,7\,|\,(x-5)\} \\  & =\{x\in Z\,:\,x=5+7k,k\in Z\} \\  & =\{…,-9,-2,5,12,19,…\}.\end{aligned}
$$

We see that $12$ and $-2$ are in $[5],$ while $-4$ is not.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

q-86223.name: Question 5
q-86223.problem:
Consider the equivalence relation $∼$ on $R,$ defined by $x∼y$ if $\sqrt[3]{x}=\sqrt[3]{y}.$ Which of the following are in the equivalence class $[-8]?$

I. $-8$

II. $8$

III. $2$
q-86223.worked_solution:
The equivalence class $[-8]$ consists of the elements that are equivalent to $-8$ under the given equivalence relation. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}[-8] & =\{x\in R\,|\,x∼-8\} \\  & =\{x\in R\,|\,\sqrt[3]{x}=\sqrt[3]{-8}\} \\  & =\{x\in R\,|\,\sqrt[3]{x}=-2\} \\  & =\{-8\}.\end{aligned}
$$

We see that $-8$ is in $[-8],$ while $8$ and $2$ are not.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only".

q-221766.name: Question 6
q-221766.problem:
Consider the equivalence relation $∼$ on $R,$ defined by $x∼y$ if $\operatorname{sin}⁡x=\operatorname{sin}⁡y.$ Which of the following equivalence classes contain the element $4\pi ?$

I. $[-\pi ]$

II. $[\frac{\pi }{2}]$

III. $[3\pi ]$
q-221766.worked_solution:
We have $4\pi \in [x]$ if $4\pi ∼x.$ Using the definition of the given equivalence relation, we require

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\pi ) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ 0 & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Let's now consider each of the given equivalence classes.

- $4\pi \in [-\pi ]$ because $\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\pi )=0\,✓$

- $4\pi \notin [\frac{\pi }{2}]$ because $\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})=1\ne 0\,\times $

- $4\pi \in [3\pi ]$ because $\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi )=0\,✓$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."
